title: Build a GPT from scratch
summary: Turn text into next-token examples, build a causal GPT in PyTorch, verify it on GPT-2's weights, train it with honest evaluation, speed it up, then sample.
outcomes: Explain why a GPT trains on every position of a sequence at once and why the causal mask is required
Trace tensor shapes through causal self-attention and compute GPT-2 small's 124M parameters from its config
Write a GPT-2 model in PyTorch and verify it by loading the released weights and matching reference logits
Choose initialization, AdamW, warmup plus cosine schedule and gradient accumulation settings and say what each prevents
Prepare token data, estimate validation loss, recognize overfitting and checkpoint and resume a run
Explain how TF32, bfloat16, torch.compile, fused attention and DDP speed up training, and compute MFU
Predict how temperature, top-k and top-p reshape the next-token distribution during sampling

lessons.title: Next-token prediction: turning raw text into training examples

blocks.md: A **GPT** (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) is a decoder-only Transformer trained on one task: given the tokens so far, predict the next one. GPT-1 (Radford et al., 2018, the first GPT paper) states the objective as maximizing the log-probability of each token $u_i$ given the $k$ tokens before it, where $k$ is the context window. Nothing else is needed for pretraining: no labels, no encoder, no second sequence.

blocks.caption: Equation 1 of the GPT-1 paper. Theta are the network weights; training pushes up the probability of every actual next token in the corpus.

blocks.md: We will build the model the way **nanoGPT** (Andrej Karpathy's open-source GPT trainer, a model file and a training loop of about 300 lines each) and Karpathy's *Let's build GPT* video lecture do. The data is **Tiny Shakespeare**, one text file holding a subset of Shakespeare's works, first released with Karpathy's char-rnn project: 1,115,394 characters with 65 distinct characters. To keep the numbers small we tokenize at the character level: sort the 65 characters and map each to its index (newline is 0, space is 1, `F` is 18, `i` is 47). The first 90% is the training split (1,003,854 tokens), the last 10% is validation (111,540). GPT-2 instead uses byte-level BPE with 50,257 tokens; nothing else in the recipe changes.

The model reads at most `block_size` tokens at a time: that is its **context length**, the $k$ of the objective above. A training example is a chunk of `block_size + 1` consecutive tokens cut at a random offset; the extra token is there so that the last input position also has a next token to predict. The figure uses `block_size` = 8; the Shakespeare config uses 256 and GPT-2 uses 1024.

blocks.title: One chunk of 9 characters holds 8 training examples

scenes.caption: Take block_size + 1 = 9 characters from a random offset ('First Cit', sp is a space). x is the first 8 ids, y is the same ids shifted left by one.
Position 0: context is just 'F' (18) and the target is 'i' (47). The model must learn to predict from a single character.
Position 3: context is 'Firs' (18 47 56 57) and the target is 't' (58). Same tensors, a longer context.
Position 7: all 8 inputs are context and the target is 't' (58). One forward pass scores all 8 predictions at once, each seeing only its own prefix.

blocks.md: A batch stacks `batch_size` such chunks into two integer tensors of shape $(B,T)$: $B$ is `batch_size`, the number of chunks, and $T$ is `block_size`, the positions per chunk (nanoGPT calls it the time axis). Every one of the $B \times T$ positions is a prediction with its own target, so the nanoGPT Shakespeare config (batch 64, block 256) trains on 16,384 next-character predictions per step. This parallelism is why Transformers train so much faster than models that must step through a sequence.

blocks.code:
data = torch.tensor(encode(text), dtype=torch.long)
n = int(0.9 * len(data))
train_data, val_data = data[:n], data[n:]

def get_batch(split):
    data = train_data if split == 'train' else val_data
    ix = torch.randint(len(data) - block_size, (batch_size,))
    x = torch.stack([data[i:i+block_size] for i in ix])
    y = torch.stack([data[i+1:i+block_size+1] for i in ix])
    return x, y   # both (batch_size, block_size)
blocks.caption: Data loading from the lecture's gpt.py: random offsets, targets are inputs shifted by one.

blocks.md: The model outputs **logits**: one unnormalized score per vocabulary entry at every position, shape $(B,T,V)$. Softmax turns each row into a distribution, and the loss is the average **cross-entropy**, the negative log-probability assigned to the true next token.

blocks.caption: z is the logit vector at one position, y the target id. nanoGPT computes this with F.cross_entropy on logits flattened to (B*T, V).

blocks.prompt: Before any training, the weights are small random numbers, so logits are close to zero at every position. What loss should the first evaluation print for the 65-character model?
blocks.reveal:
Near-zero logits give a near-uniform softmax, so every target gets probability about $1/65$ and the loss is $-\ln(1/65)=\ln 65 \approx 4.17$. For GPT-2's 50,257 tokens it is $\ln 50257 \approx 10.82$.

This is a free sanity check: a first loss far above $\ln V$ means the initialization is producing confident wrong guesses, which wastes the first part of training.

blocks.md:
The unit of this loss is the **nat**. Cross-entropy here uses the natural log, and information measured with natural logs is counted in nats; with log base 2 it would be bits, and one nat is $1/\ln 2 \approx 1.44$ bits. So the untrained model pays 4.17 nats per character.

The same number has a second reading, **perplexity**: undo the log by raising $e$ to the loss, and you get the number of equally likely choices the model is effectively torn between. At initialization $e^{\ln 65} = 65$, as unsure as a uniform pick among all 65 characters; a perfect model would reach perplexity 1. Papers often report perplexity instead of loss, and lower is better for both.

blocks.title: Cross-entropy is minus the log-probability of the target

scenes.caption: Untrained: uniform over 65 characters gives p = 0.015 and loss ln 65 = 4.17.
Halfway confident: p = 0.5 gives loss ln 2 = 0.69. The loss falls fast as probability climbs from tiny values.
Confident and right: p = 0.9 gives loss 0.11. Loss only reaches 0 if the model puts all mass on the target, which real text never allows.

blocks.md: Before any Transformer, the lecture trains the simplest model that fits this setup, a **bigram** model (*bi* for two: it only ever looks at a pair of adjacent characters). It predicts the next character from the current character alone. The whole model is one `nn.Embedding(65, 65)` table: row $i$ holds the 65 logits for whatever follows character $i$, so it has $65 \times 65 = 4{,}225$ parameters and no context beyond one character.

blocks.code:
class BigramLanguageModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size):
        super().__init__()
        # row i holds the logits for the character after character i
        self.token_embedding_table = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, vocab_size)

    def forward(self, idx, targets=None):
        logits = self.token_embedding_table(idx)        # (B, T, 65)
        if targets is None:
            return logits, None
        B, T, C = logits.shape
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(B*T, C), targets.view(B*T))
        return logits, loss

model = BigramLanguageModel(65)
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
for it in range(3000):
    xb, yb = get_batch('train')          # 32 chunks of 8 characters
    logits, loss = model(xb, yb)
    optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

scenes.caption: Step 0: 4.73 on both splits, above the 4.17 of a uniform guess. nn.Embedding starts from a standard normal, so the first logits are large and confidently wrong.
Step 300: 2.81 train, 2.82 val. One lookup table already learns which characters tend to follow which.

blocks.md: Two things to read off that log. The first loss is 4.73, not 4.17: `nn.Embedding` initializes its table from a standard normal distribution (standard deviation 1), so the starting logits are far from zero and confidently wrong, the symptom in the second quiz below (the lecture's first loss, on one batch before training, was 4.87). And the loss stalls near 2.49 after about 1,000 steps. The training loop works; what is missing is context. Every later piece, from attention to stacked blocks, has to beat this number, and lesson 4 shows how much each one buys.

Training is **teacher forcing on every position in parallel**: the true previous tokens are always the context, and all $B \times T$ predictions are scored in one pass. Generation is the opposite, one token at a time feeding its own outputs back in.

`block_size` is the **maximum** context, not the only context. Because position $t$ in each chunk sees only $t+1$ tokens, the model is trained on every context length from 1 to `block_size`, which is exactly what it needs when generation starts from a short prompt.

blocks.question: nanoGPT's GPT-2 config uses micro-batches (a micro-batch is the group of sequences that goes through the model in one forward pass) of 12 sequences of 1024 tokens. How many next-token predictions does one micro-batch contribute to the loss?
options: 12,288, one per position of every sequence
12, one per sequence
1,024, one per position
1,023 x 12, because the last token has no target
blocks.explain: Targets are the inputs shifted by one, and the loader reads block_size + 1 tokens, so every one of the 12 x 1024 = 12,288 positions has a target. Only the final position of the whole dataset lacks one, which is why ix is drawn below len(data) - block_size.

blocks.question: A teammate's first logged loss on the 65-character model is 27. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The model is already overfitting
The data loader is shifting targets by two
The initialization makes some logits huge, so the model is confidently wrong
Nothing: 27 is typical for an untrained character model
blocks.explain: An untrained model with small weights should print about ln 65 = 4.17. A much larger loss means a very low probability on the true token, which only happens when logits are large and spread out, typically from weights initialized with too large a scale.

lessons.title: Causal self-attention: each position may only look backward

blocks.md: Recall from the attention course: self-attention lets each position build its output as a weighted average of value vectors from other positions, with weights from a softmax over query-key scores. In a GPT that freedom is a problem. Position $t$ is trained to predict token $t+1$, and token $t+1$ is sitting in the input right next to it.

The fix is a **causal mask**: before the softmax, every score where the key position is later than the query position is set to $-\infty$, so its weight becomes exactly 0. Karpathy's lecture builds this up from the simplest case, plain averaging of the past, which turns out to be a matrix multiply with a lower-triangular matrix (`torch.tril`).

blocks.title: From scores to causal attention weights on 4 positions

scenes.caption: Start with every score equal to 0: each query rates every key the same. Rows are queries (the position doing the looking), columns are keys.
Mask the upper triangle (key later than query) with minus infinity. Row 0 may look only at itself; row 3 may look at all four.
Softmax each row. Equal scores over the allowed keys give a plain running average: 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4. This is tril(ones) with each row normalized.
Now use data-dependent scores (made-up toy numbers; a trained model computes them as q dot k divided by sqrt of head size).
Softmax again: row i puts 0.88 on itself, row s puts 0.53 on F. Weights still sum to 1 per row and are exactly 0 above the diagonal.

blocks.md: Apply both weight matrices to toy one-dimensional values $v = (4, 2, 6, 0)$. The uniform weights give the running means $(4, 3, 4, 3)$. The learned weights give $(4, 2.24, 4.84, 2.96)$: each output is still built only from its own past, but the mix is now chosen by content. Row 0 always copies its own value, because it has nothing else to see.

blocks.caption: Causal attention: softmax of Q K transpose over the square root of d_h, plus the mask M, times V. d_h is the head size; M is 0 where key j is at or before query i and minus infinity after it. This is nanoGPT's masked_fill(tril == 0, -inf).

blocks.prompt: You forget the mask and train the character model. What do the training loss and the generated samples look like?
blocks.reveal: The training loss drops far below anything an honest model reaches, because position $t$ can attend to token $t+1$, which *is* its target, and simply copy it. At generation time there is no future token to copy, so samples are garbage. A suspiciously low training loss is the classic symptom of a leaking mask.

blocks.md: Now the real shapes. nanoGPT names the axes of its activations $(B, T, C)$: batch, time (position) and **channels**, where $C$ is the width of the vector at each position (`n_embd`, 768 in GPT-2 small). Attention splits those 768 channels into `n_head` = 12 heads of 64. A **micro-batch** is the group of sequences that goes through one forward and backward pass; lesson 5 explains why GPT-2 training adds up the gradients of 40 of them before each weight update.

blocks.title: Shapes through nanoGPT's CausalSelfAttention (GPT-2 small)
blocks.code:
def forward(self, x):
    B, T, C = x.size()
    q, k, v = self.c_attn(x).split(self.n_embd, dim=2)
    k = k.view(B, T, nh, C // nh).transpose(1, 2)
    q = q.view(B, T, nh, C // nh).transpose(1, 2)
    v = v.view(B, T, nh, C // nh).transpose(1, 2)
    att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) * (1.0 / math.sqrt(k.size(-1)))
    att = att.masked_fill(self.bias[:,:,:T,:T] == 0, float('-inf'))
    att = F.softmax(att, dim=-1)
    y = att @ v
    y = y.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, T, C)
    return self.resid_dropout(self.c_proj(y))

scenes.caption: Input: a micro-batch of 12 sequences, 1024 positions, 768 channels.
One fused Linear (c_attn, 768 to 2304) computes queries, keys and values for all heads; split cuts it into three 768-wide pieces.
Reshape 768 channels into 12 heads of 64 and move the head axis forward so every head is processed like an extra batch dimension.
Scores for every head: a 1024 x 1024 matrix per head, scaled by 1/sqrt(64) = 0.125.
The causal mask and the row softmax: future positions get weight 0.
Weighted sum of values, then heads are laid back side by side into 768 channels and mixed by the output projection c_proj.

blocks.md: That `att` tensor holds $12 \times 12 \times 1024 \times 1024 = 150{,}994{,}944$ numbers, about 302 MB at 2 bytes per 16-bit float, for one layer of one micro-batch. So nanoGPT normally skips lines 7 to 10 and calls PyTorch's `scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)`, which can use a Flash Attention kernel (one fused GPU routine that walks over blocks of keys in fast on-chip memory, keeping a running softmax) that computes the same result without materializing the $T \times T$ matrix. The manual path is kept as a fallback and is the clearest statement of the math. Lesson 7 shows what the fused kernel buys in step time.

The causal mask is the only thing that makes this a *decoder*. Remove it and you have an encoder block; keep it and every position's prediction depends only on its prefix, so one pass trains all $T$ positions honestly.

blocks.question: A bug report: the mask was built with `torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T))` instead of `torch.tril(...)`, keeping the `masked_fill(mask == 0, -inf)` line unchanged. What does position 0 attend to now?
options: Only itself, as before
All positions 0 to T-1, including the future
Nothing, so its row is all minus infinity
Only position T-1
blocks.explain: triu keeps the upper triangle, so row 0 keeps columns 0 to T-1 and the model sees the whole future from the first position. The last row is the one that keeps just one key, its own. The loss will look great and generation will fail.

blocks.question: Why does nanoGPT compute q, k and v for all 12 heads with one 768-to-2304 Linear instead of 36 small ones?
options: It is mathematically different and gives better accuracy
GPT-2 heads share their key matrices
It halves the parameter count
One large matrix multiply uses the GPU far better than many small ones, and gives the same result
blocks.explain: Stacking the per-head projection matrices side by side is the same linear map, so the outputs are identical. The gain is purely efficiency: one large matmul instead of many small launches. Parameter count is the same 768 x 2304 weights either way.

lessons.title: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head

blocks.md: A GPT block does two things, which the lecture code describes as *communication followed by computation*. Causal self-attention moves information **between** positions. Then a feed-forward **MLP** (multi-layer perceptron) processes each position **independently**: a Linear layer expanding the width 4 times (768 to 3072 in GPT-2 small, the same 3072 GPT-1 used), a GELU nonlinearity, and a Linear layer back to 768.

**GELU** (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016) multiplies each input by a probability, $\operatorname{GELU}(x) = x\,\Phi(x)$, where $\Phi(x)$ is the probability that a standard normal sample falls below $x$. Its full name, Gaussian Error Linear Unit, comes from that Gaussian: $\Phi$ is written with the error function erf. Each input is scaled by its own $\Phi$: $\operatorname{GELU}(1) = 1 \times 0.841 = 0.841$, while $\operatorname{GELU}(-1) = -1 \times 0.159 = -0.159$. Far from zero it acts like ReLU (about $x$ for large positive inputs, about 0 for large negative ones), but it bends smoothly near zero instead of having a kink. GPT-1 and GPT-2 both use it, but OpenAI's released GPT-2 code computes the **tanh approximation** below rather than $\Phi$ itself. nanoGPT calls the exact `nn.GELU()`; Karpathy's later GPT-2 reproduction, build-nanogpt, uses `nn.GELU(approximate='tanh')` to match the released weights, which matters in lesson 4.

blocks.caption: The gelu function in openai/gpt-2's model.py, and PyTorch's approximate='tanh'. At x = 1 it gives 0.84119 against the exact 0.84134; the two never differ by more than about 0.0005 at the points we checked.

blocks.md: Each sub-layer is wrapped in a **residual connection**: its output is added to its input, so the activations form a *residual stream* that every block reads from and writes back into. **LayerNorm**, from the prerequisite course, rescales each position's vector to mean 0 and variance 1 across its channels, then multiplies by a learned gain and adds a learned shift. GPT-2 moved LayerNorm to the **input** of each sub-block (pre-LN) and added one final LayerNorm after the last block. The original Transformer put LayerNorm after the addition (post-LN).

blocks.caption: nanoGPT's Block.forward, line for line. With pre-LN the stream itself is never normalized, so the identity path from embeddings to output stays clean.

blocks.md: One more piece appears only when the config sets `dropout` above 0 (lesson 6 shows when that helps). nanoGPT then applies dropout in three kinds of places: to the sum of token and position embeddings, to the attention weights after the softmax, and to the output of each sub-layer (after `c_proj` in attention and in the MLP) just before it is added to the residual stream. The stream itself is never dropped directly, so the identity path stays intact.

Now the whole model. It starts with two learned lookup tables, named `wte` and `wpe` after the variables in OpenAI's GPT-2 code. `wte` is the token embedding table, one row of $C$ numbers per vocabulary entry; `wpe` is the position embedding table, one row per position from 0 to the maximum context minus 1. At the end, `lm_head` (the language-model head) is a Linear layer from $C$ to $V$ that turns each final vector into one logit per vocabulary entry.

blocks.title: The whole GPT forward pass in nanoGPT

scenes.caption: Token ids index a learned table wte; positions 0 to T-1 index a second learned table wpe. GPT uses learned position embeddings, not sinusoids.
The two lookups are added: each position starts as a 768-dim vector that knows what it is and where it is. This sum is the start of the residual stream.
Twelve identical blocks (different weights) each add an attention update and an MLP update to the stream. Shape stays (B, T, 768) throughout.
A final LayerNorm, then lm_head maps each 768-dim vector to 50,257 logits, one score per possible next token.
Weight tying: lm_head.weight and wte.weight are the same tensor. Mapping tokens to vectors and vectors back to token scores share one 38.6M-parameter matrix.
Training: logits at all B x T positions meet the shifted targets in cross-entropy. At inference nanoGPT runs lm_head only on the last position.

blocks.md: Weight tying is old: GPT-1 already writes the output as $P(u)=\operatorname{softmax}(h_n W_e^{\top})$ where $h_n$ is the last block's output and $W_e$ is the same matrix used to embed tokens, and Press and Wolf showed that tying input and output embeddings lowers perplexity (lesson 1: $e$ raised to the loss) while cutting parameters. The intuition: a token that is a good *input* match for a context vector should also be a good *output* prediction for it.

Count GPT-2 small's parameters ($V=50257$ vocabulary entries, $T_{max}=1024$ positions, $C=768$ channels, $L=12$ blocks, biases on). Per block: attention has four $C \times C$ matrices (q, k, v and the output projection), each with a bias of $C$, so $4C^2+4C$. The MLP has a $C \times 4C$ matrix with a $4C$ bias and a $4C \times C$ matrix with a $C$ bias, so $8C^2+5C$. Each of the two LayerNorms has a gain and a shift of $C$ numbers, $4C$ in all. That is $12C^2+13C = 7{,}087{,}872$ per block.

blocks.caption: N adds the token table V x C, the position table T_max x C, L blocks of 12 C squared plus 13 C, and 2C for the final LayerNorm. Without tying, a separate lm_head would add another V x C = 38,597,376.

blocks.title: Where GPT-2 small's parameters live (millions)

scenes.caption: Tied model: 124.44M total. The MLPs hold 45.5%, the token table 31.0%, attention 22.8%. LayerNorms are only 38,400 parameters.
Untied: a separate output matrix adds 38.6M, a model of 163.04M that is 31% larger for the same compute per block.

blocks.md: Running the same count for the larger GPT-2 shapes (24 x 1024, 36 x 1280, 48 x 1600) gives 354.8M, 774.0M and 1557.6M. The GPT-2 paper's Table 2 lists 117M, 345M, 762M and 1542M; nanoGPT counts the released checkpoints' tensors and so calls the smallest one 124M. nanoGPT also pads the vocabulary to 50,304 (786 x 64) when training from scratch, because matrix sizes that are multiples of 64 run faster on GPUs.

blocks.prompt: You double the width $C$ from 768 to 1536 and keep 12 layers. Roughly how much do the block parameters grow?
blocks.reveal: About **4 times**: block parameters scale as $12C^2$, so $7{,}087{,}872$ becomes $28{,}331{,}520$ per block (a ratio of 3.997). The embedding table only doubles, since it is $V \times C$. This is why width is the expensive knob.

blocks.md: Pre-LN vs post-LN is not cosmetic. Xiong et al. show that in the original post-LN Transformer the gradients near the output are large at initialization, which is why it needs a careful learning-rate warmup. Placing LayerNorm inside the residual branch, as GPT-2 does, gives well-behaved gradients at initialization.

A GPT is just: embed (token + position), $L$ x [pre-LN causal attention, pre-LN MLP, each added to the residual stream], final LayerNorm, project back to vocabulary scores with the tied embedding matrix.

blocks.question: In nanoGPT's Block, where is LayerNorm applied?
options: After each residual addition, x = LN(x + attn(x))
On the input to each sub-layer, x = x + attn(LN(x)), plus one final ln_f
Only once, before the first block
Only on the attention scores before the softmax
blocks.explain: GPT-2 moved LayerNorm to the input of each sub-block and added a final LayerNorm after the last block. The first option is the post-LN layout of the 2017 Transformer.

blocks.question: For GPT-2 small, roughly what share of all parameters sits in the MLPs?
options: About 10%
About 23%
About 45%
About 31%
blocks.explain: The MLPs have 8C^2 + 5C per block, twice attention's 4C^2 + 4C, totalling 56.67M of 124.44M, which is 45.5%. 23% is attention and 31% is the token embedding table.

lessons.title: Assemble model.py and check it against GPT-2's real weights

blocks.md: Lessons 1 to 3 met every piece of a GPT one at a time. Now we write them down as one file, in the order nanoGPT and Karpathy's *Let's reproduce GPT-2* lecture (its code is the build-nanogpt repo) do, and then prove the file right. The proof is simple: OpenAI released GPT-2's trained weights, so if our model loads them and produces the same logits as a trusted implementation on the same prompt, every shape, layer order and constant must be correct. A bug as small as a missing transpose shows up as wrong numbers.

The names are not arbitrary. `c_attn`, `c_proj`, `c_fc`, `ln_1`, `wte` and `wpe` are the variable names in OpenAI's GPT-2 code, kept by the Hugging Face `transformers` library (which hosts the weights as a PyTorch **state dict**: a dictionary from each parameter's dotted name, such as `transformer.h.0.attn.c_attn.weight`, to its tensor). Matching the names means loading is a loop over keys. First the configuration and attention, which you saw as a shape trace in lesson 2:

blocks.code:
import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
import torch, torch.nn as nn
from torch.nn import functional as F

@dataclass
class GPTConfig:
    block_size: int = 1024   # max context length
    vocab_size: int = 50257  # GPT-2 BPE vocabulary
    n_layer: int = 12
    n_head: int = 12
    n_embd: int = 768
    dropout: float = 0.0

class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, cfg):
        super().__init__()
        self.c_attn = nn.Linear(cfg.n_embd, 3 * cfg.n_embd)  # q, k, v, all heads
        self.c_proj = nn.Linear(cfg.n_embd, cfg.n_embd)      # writes to the stream
        self.n_head, self.n_embd = cfg.n_head, cfg.n_embd
        self.resid_dropout = nn.Dropout(cfg.dropout)
        self.dropout = cfg.dropout                          # for attention weights

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.size()
        q, k, v = self.c_attn(x).split(self.n_embd, dim=2)
        q = q.view(B, T, self.n_head, C // self.n_head).transpose(1, 2)
        k = k.view(B, T, self.n_head, C // self.n_head).transpose(1, 2)
        v = v.view(B, T, self.n_head, C // self.n_head).transpose(1, 2)
        y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True,
                dropout_p=self.dropout if self.training else 0.0)
        y = y.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, T, C)
        return self.resid_dropout(self.c_proj(y))
blocks.caption: GPTConfig and CausalSelfAttention, following build-nanogpt's train_gpt2.py (we added the optional dropout). One fused Linear makes q, k and v; scaled_dot_product_attention with is_causal=True applies the causal mask from lesson 2.
The MLP (768 to 3072 to 768 with tanh-approximate GELU) and the pre-LN Block from lesson 3: two residual additions, each reading a LayerNorm-ed copy of the stream.

blocks.code:
class GPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, cfg):
        super().__init__()
        self.config = cfg
        self.transformer = nn.ModuleDict(dict(
            wte=nn.Embedding(cfg.vocab_size, cfg.n_embd),
            wpe=nn.Embedding(cfg.block_size, cfg.n_embd),
            drop=nn.Dropout(cfg.dropout),
            h=nn.ModuleList([Block(cfg) for _ in range(cfg.n_layer)]),
            ln_f=nn.LayerNorm(cfg.n_embd)))
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(cfg.n_embd, cfg.vocab_size, bias=False)
        self.transformer.wte.weight = self.lm_head.weight   # weight tying
        self.apply(self._init_weights)                      # N(0, 0.02), zero biases
        for name, p in self.named_parameters():
            if name.endswith('c_proj.weight'):              # 0.02 / sqrt(2L)
                nn.init.normal_(p, 0.0, 0.02 / math.sqrt(2 * cfg.n_layer))

    def forward(self, idx, targets=None):
        B, T = idx.size()
        pos = torch.arange(T, device=idx.device)
        x = self.transformer.wte(idx) + self.transformer.wpe(pos)
        x = self.transformer.drop(x)
        for block in self.transformer.h:
            x = block(x)
        logits = self.lm_head(self.transformer.ln_f(x))      # (B, T, V)
        loss = None
        if targets is not None:
            loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, logits.size(-1)), targets.view(-1))
        return logits, loss

blocks.md: Two checks need no weights at all. Counting parameters with `sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())` must give lesson 3's 124,439,808; PyTorch counts a tied tensor once, since `parameters()` skips duplicates. And the first loss of a fresh model should be near $\ln 50257 \approx 10.82$ (lesson 1). Then come the released weights, with one wrinkle: OpenAI's code implemented every Linear layer as a 1-D convolution (`Conv1D`) whose weight is stored as (in, out), while PyTorch's `nn.Linear` stores (out, in) and computes $xW^{\top}$. So the four matrix weights of each block must be transposed on the way in.

blocks.code:
@classmethod
def from_pretrained(cls, name='gpt2'):
    from transformers import GPT2LMHeadModel
    model = cls(GPTConfig())                    # random init, right shapes
    sd = model.state_dict()
    sd_hf = GPT2LMHeadModel.from_pretrained(name).state_dict()
    # older transformers versions also store the causal mask as buffers
    keys = [k for k in sd_hf if not k.endswith(('.attn.bias', '.attn.masked_bias'))]
    assert len(keys) == len(sd)
    conv1d = ('attn.c_attn.weight', 'attn.c_proj.weight',
              'mlp.c_fc.weight', 'mlp.c_proj.weight')
    with torch.no_grad():
        for k in keys:
            if k.endswith(conv1d):              # stored as (in, out): transpose
                assert sd_hf[k].shape[::-1] == sd[k].shape
                sd[k].copy_(sd_hf[k].t())
            else:
                assert sd_hf[k].shape == sd[k].shape
                sd[k].copy_(sd_hf[k])
    return model
blocks.caption: from_pretrained, a method inside class GPT, after nanoGPT and build-nanogpt. The four Conv1D weights per block, 48 tensors in all, are transposed; everything else (embeddings, LayerNorms, biases) copies as is.

scenes.caption: Start from lesson 1's bigram baseline: about 2.5 nats per character on Tiny Shakespeare with one character of context.
A single causal self-attention head reaches about 2.4; four smaller heads side by side, 2.28.

blocks.md: The figure is the payoff of lesson 1's baseline: each component is judged by how far it pushes validation loss below 2.5, and the biggest single step comes from scale once the architecture is right. That is also the order to debug in. A model that cannot beat the bigram has a broken loop or mask; a model that loads GPT-2's weights but disagrees with the reference has a broken layer.

Our exact-GELU variant is a quieter case. Swapping `approximate='tanh'` for the exact `nn.GELU()` (nanoGPT's default) and loading the same weights, the largest logit difference was 0.080 and every argmax still matched. That is close but not equal: GPT-2's weights were trained through the tanh formula, so only the tanh version reproduces the reference to the last bit. For training from scratch either GELU is fine.

Before training a from-scratch model, load the released GPT-2 weights into it and compare logits against a reference on a fixed prompt. A difference of zero (or float noise) proves the architecture; anything visibly larger means a wrong layer, a missing transpose or a different activation.

blocks.question: Your from-scratch GPT-2 small reports 163,037,184 parameters. What did you most likely get wrong?
options: The MLP is 8 times wider than the embedding, not 4
You counted the attention mask buffers as parameters
lm_head has its own weight matrix instead of sharing wte's
The position table has 2,048 rows instead of 1,024
blocks.explain: The excess is 163,037,184 - 124,439,808 = 38,597,376 = 50,257 x 768, exactly one extra token-sized matrix. That is an untied lm_head. A doubled position table would add only 786,432, and buffers are not parameters.

blocks.question: After loading GPT-2's weights, your logits differ from Hugging Face's by at most 0.08 and every argmax agrees. Which cause fits best?
options: A missing transpose on attn.c_proj
The MLP uses exact GELU while GPT-2 was trained with the tanh approximation
Weight tying is missing
The causal mask is upper-triangular
blocks.explain: The two GELU formulas differ by a few ten-thousandths per activation, which adds up to small logit differences that rarely change the argmax; that is what we measured (0.080). A missing transpose gave a difference of 161.7 and degenerate text, and a flipped mask would leak the future and change the logits wildly.

lessons.title: Training it: initialization, AdamW and a warmup plus cosine schedule

blocks.md: The architecture is done; the rest is careful deep-net practice from the prerequisite course. nanoGPT initializes every Linear and Embedding weight from $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.02^2)$, a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 0.02, and every bias at zero, the same $\mathcal{N}(0,0.02)$ GPT-1 reports. That 0.02 is a fixed choice, not derived from the width: a fan-in rule such as $1/\sqrt{C}$ would give 0.036 for $C=768$. One exception comes from GPT-2: the projections that write into the residual stream (`c_proj` in attention and in the MLP) are scaled down by $1/\sqrt{n_{res}}$, where $n_{res}$ is the number of residual layers, that is, of additions into the stream.

blocks.prompt: GPT-2 small has 12 blocks, each with 2 residual additions. What standard deviation does nanoGPT use for c_proj weights, and why shrink them at all?
blocks.reveal:
$0.02/\sqrt{2 \cdot 12} = 0.02/\sqrt{24} \approx 0.0041$.

Each residual addition adds a roughly independent random contribution, so at initialization the variance of the stream grows with the number of additions: variances of independent terms add, so 24 additions of variance $\sigma^2$ give $24\sigma^2$. Scaling the writers by $1/\sqrt{24}$ divides each contribution's variance by 24, so the total, $24 \times \sigma^2/24 = \sigma^2$, stays roughly the size of a single contribution and deeper models start in the same regime as shallow ones. The GPT-2 paper describes it as accounting for accumulation on the residual path with depth.

blocks.md: The optimizer is **AdamW** (the W is for decoupled weight decay: Adam with weight decay applied directly to the weights, decoupled from the gradient step, per Loshchilov and Hutter). nanoGPT's GPT-2 settings: $\beta_1=0.9$, $\beta_2=0.95$, weight decay 0.1, gradient norm clipped at 1.0. $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ are the decay rates of Adam's moving averages of the gradient and of the squared gradient; an average with decay $\beta$ remembers roughly the last $1/(1-\beta)$ steps, so 0.9 means about 10 steps and 0.95 about 20. Clipping at 1.0 means that if the norm of all gradients together exceeds 1.0, every gradient is scaled down so that norm is exactly 1.0. Weight decay goes only to tensors with 2 or more dimensions (matmul weights and embeddings); biases and LayerNorm gains are not decayed.

Batch size is counted in tokens. nanoGPT's GPT-2 run uses micro-batches of 12 x 1024 tokens and accumulates gradients over 40 of them (5 per GPU on 8 GPUs, whose gradients are averaged) before each optimizer step: $12 \times 1024 \times 40 = 491{,}520$ tokens per step. A batch that size does not fit in one GPU's memory, so **gradient accumulation** splits it: run forward and backward on one micro-batch with its loss divided by the number of micro-batches, add its gradients to a running sum, repeat, and only then update the weights. Because of that division the sum is the average gradient, the same step as one big batch. 600,000 steps is about 294.9 billion tokens, the "300B" in the config. GPT-2 itself used batches of 512 sequences of 1024 tokens.

blocks.code:
optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
for micro_step in range(grad_accum_steps):    # 40 in nanoGPT's GPT-2 config
    x, y = get_batch('train')
    logits, loss = model(x, y)
    loss = loss / grad_accum_steps            # each micro-batch is a 1/40 share
    loss.backward()                           # gradients add up in .grad
torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
optimizer.step()
blocks.caption: The micro-step loop of nanoGPT's train.py and build-nanogpt, without the mixed precision and multi-GPU lines that lesson 7 adds. The division makes the summed gradient the mean over all 491,520 tokens.
nanoGPT's get_lr: linear warmup for w steps, then cosine decay to eta_min at step D. GPT defaults: eta_max 6e-4, w 2000, D 600,000, eta_min 6e-5.

blocks.md: In words, $\eta$ is the learning rate and $t$ the step. During warmup ($t<w$) the rate climbs in a straight line, $\eta_{max}(t+1)/(w+1)$, so step 1,000 of 2,000 runs at about half the peak. After warmup, $r$ is the fraction of the decay finished, from 0 to 1. The factor $\frac{1}{2}(1+\cos \pi r)$ follows half a cosine wave from 1 at $r=0$ (rate $\eta_{max}$) through one half at $r=0.5$ to 0 at $r=1$ (rate $\eta_{min}$). With the defaults the midpoint rate is $(6\times10^{-4}+6\times10^{-5})/2 = 3.3\times10^{-4}$.

The README reports about 3 minutes on one A100 GPU (an NVIDIA data-center GPU), and a best validation loss of 1.4697.

The GPT-2 numbers in the next figure come from **OpenWebText** (OWT), an open re-creation by Gokaslan and Cohen of **WebText**, the dataset OpenAI built for GPT-2 and never released. WebText is the text of about 8 million web pages (40 GB) linked from Reddit posts that received at least 3 karma, a cheap filter for pages people found worth sharing. nanoGPT's prepared OpenWebText holds about 9 billion GPT-2 tokens for training. All losses here are in nats per token, as in lesson 1.

blocks.title: Reported losses in nats per token (lower is better)

scenes.caption: Character level: from 4.17 untrained to 1.88 for the small CPU config and 1.47 for the 3-minute GPU run (nanoGPT README).
GPT-2 BPE tokens on OpenWebText: 10.82 untrained; the released 124M checkpoint scores 3.12 val, and nanoGPT's 124M run reaches about 2.85 after roughly 4 days on 8 A100s.

blocks.md: Never compare losses across tokenizers. 1.47 nats per *character* and 2.85 nats per *BPE token* measure different things: a BPE token covers several characters, so it is much harder to predict. The released GPT-2 scores 3.12 on OWT partly because it was trained on WebText, not OpenWebText; nanoGPT notes that fine-tuning it on OWT brings it to about 2.85.

How much compute is that? A **FLOP** counts one arithmetic step on floating-point numbers, a multiply or an add. nanoGPT's MFU (model FLOPs utilization: achieved FLOPs as a share of the GPU's peak) estimate counts $6N + 12\,L\,H\,d_h\,T$ FLOPs per token, following the PaLM paper, where $N$ is the parameter count (nanoGPT leaves out the position table, so about 123.7M). Where $6N$ comes from: in the forward pass each weight multiplies one input and adds the product to a sum, 2 FLOPs per weight per token, so $2N$. The backward pass computes two gradients for every matrix multiply, one for its input and one for its weights, each as costly as the forward, so $4N$ more.

The second term is attention's own arithmetic, which has no weights. Per layer and head, one token's query is dotted with $T$ keys ($2\,d_h\,T$ FLOPs; the formula counts all $T$, as PaLM does, although the causal mask leaves about half of them unused) and the $T$ values are summed with those weights (another $2\,d_h\,T$), so $4\,d_h\,T$ forward and three times that with the backward: $12\,d_h\,T$, over $H$ heads of size $d_h$ (64, which nanoGPT's code calls `Q`) and $L$ layers. For the 124M model at $T=1024$ that is about 855 million FLOPs per token, so $4.2\times10^{14}$ per optimizer step (times 491,520 tokens) and about $2.5\times10^{20}$ for the whole run (times 600,000 steps). Lesson 7 divides FLOPs like these by a measured step time to get the MFU.

The training loop is the generic one (forward, cross-entropy, backward, clip, AdamW step), and the GPT-specific knowledge is in the settings: small normal init with scaled residual projections, decoupled weight decay on matrices only, warmup then cosine decay, and big token batches via gradient accumulation.

blocks.question: Which parameters does nanoGPT's configure_optimizers exclude from weight decay?
options: The token embedding table, because it is tied
All attention weights
Nothing; AdamW decays every tensor equally
Tensors with fewer than 2 dimensions: biases and LayerNorm weights
blocks.explain: The rule is p.dim() >= 2 gets weight_decay, everything else gets 0. So matmul weights and embeddings (including the tied wte) are decayed, while 1-D biases and LayerNorm gains and shifts are not.

blocks.question: You start GPT-2 small at the peak rate 6e-4 with no warmup and the loss spikes to NaN within 100 steps. Which change addresses the cause most directly?
options: Increase weight decay to 1.0
Add a linear warmup over the first few thousand steps
Remove gradient clipping
Switch from cosine decay to a constant rate
blocks.explain: In the first steps Adam's running statistics are still settling, so full-size updates can blow up a freshly initialized model. Warmup ramps the step size meanwhile, which is why nanoGPT warms up for 2,000 steps. Xiong et al. find pre-LN models like GPT-2 less fragile here than post-LN ones, but warmup remains the standard fix. Removing clipping or raising decay does not touch the cause, and the decay shape only matters later.

blocks.question: You delete the line `loss = loss / grad_accum_steps` from a GPT run that uses AdamW and clips the gradient norm at 1.0. What changes?
options: The effective learning rate becomes grad_accum_steps times larger and the run diverges
The gradients become grad_accum_steps times smaller
The updates barely change, since Adam divides by the gradient's running scale, but the gradient norm is now grad_accum_steps times too big, so clipping fires on almost every step
Nothing at all, because each micro-batch loss is already a mean
blocks.explain: We tried it on a 2-layer character GPT with 8 micro-steps for 200 AdamW steps: validation loss 2.398 with or without the division, but clipping fired on all 200 steps instead of 51. With plain SGD (lr 0.5, no clipping) the same mistake diverged to NaN. The prerequisite course's rule (learning rate times the number of micro-steps) is the SGD story; with Adam the main damage is a clip threshold that no longer means what you set.

blocks.question: A friend's character-level model reaches 1.3 val loss and a colleague's BPE model 2.9. Which is better?
options: They cannot be compared: one is nats per character, the other nats per token
The character model, since 1.3 is lower
The BPE model, since 2.9 is higher
They are equal after dividing by ln 2
blocks.explain: Cross-entropy is measured per token, and the two tokenizers define different tokens over the same text. To compare you would need a per-character or per-byte measure on the same data.

lessons.title: The training loop end to end: data, evals, overfitting, checkpoints

blocks.md: A tiny experiment first. We gave a 0.8M-parameter character GPT only the first 100,000 characters of Tiny Shakespeare to train on (validation used the usual 111,540-character split) and trained it for 3,000 steps on a laptop CPU. By step 1,000 its validation loss had bottomed out at 2.25; by step 3,000 its training loss had fallen to 0.80 while validation loss had *risen* to 2.82. It had started memorizing its training text. This lesson builds the loop that lets you see that happen, and the habits (good data files, honest evaluation, dropout, checkpoints) that keep it from ruining a run.

Start with the data. nanoGPT prepares each dataset once into flat binary files. For Shakespeare, `data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py` builds the 65-character vocabulary, saves the two lookup dictionaries in `meta.pkl` (`stoi`, string to integer, and `itos`, integer to string, so sampling can decode later), and writes the 90/10 split as `train.bin` and `val.bin`: raw arrays of **uint16**, unsigned 16-bit integers that hold 0 to 65,535. Our `train.bin` is 2,007,708 bytes, two per token for 1,003,854 tokens.

For GPT-2's BPE, `data/openwebtext/prepare.py` does the same at scale. It encodes every document with `tiktoken`'s `gpt2` encoding using `encode_ordinary`, which treats any `<|endoftext|>` string inside the text as plain characters (tiktoken splits it into 7 ordinary tokens), then appends the real end-of-text token, id 50256, after each document. All documents are concatenated into one stream: about 9.04 billion tokens in a 17 GB `train.bin` and 4.4 million in `val.bin`. uint16 suffices because the largest GPT-2 id, 50,256, is below 65,536; a vocabulary of 100,000 would need 32-bit ids and double the file.

blocks.title: Documents become one token stream; chunks ignore the seams

scenes.caption: Three tiny documents encoded with GPT-2's tokenizer (leading spaces belong to the tokens: ' cat' is 3797). Each gets 50256 appended.
Every id fits in 16 bits, so the whole stream is stored as 2 bytes per token and read straight from disk.
get_batch cuts block_size + 1 = 9 tokens at a random offset, here 2. The chunk runs from ' sat' through the end-of-text token into the next document.
nanoGPT does not mask across the seam. Positions after 50256 may attend to the previous document; the model simply learns that text after end-of-text starts afresh.

blocks.code:
def get_batch(split):
    # re-opened every call; nanoGPT notes this avoids a memory leak
    data = np.memmap(f'data/{split}.bin', dtype=np.uint16, mode='r')
    ix = torch.randint(len(data) - block_size, (batch_size,))
    x = torch.stack([torch.from_numpy(data[i:i+block_size].astype(np.int64)) for i in ix])
    y = torch.stack([torch.from_numpy(data[i+1:i+1+block_size].astype(np.int64)) for i in ix])
    return x.to(device), y.to(device)
blocks.caption: nanoGPT's get_batch. np.memmap maps the file into memory without reading it: the operating system loads only the pages that the random slices touch, so a 17 GB file costs almost no RAM.

blocks.md: Next, evaluation. A loss computed on one batch is noisy: for the final checkpoint of the dropout run below, 400 single-batch validation losses (32 chunks of 64 characters each) had a mean of 2.263 but ranged from 2.01 to 2.51, a standard deviation of 0.085. Averaging $n$ batches shrinks that by $\sqrt{n}$, to about 0.019 for 20 batches and 0.006 for nanoGPT's default 200. Even so, an estimate is not exact: when we reloaded the step-1,000 checkpoint, the fresh 100-batch estimate read 2.271 against the 2.248 saved with it.

blocks.caption: nanoGPT's estimate_loss. model.eval() switches dropout off so the estimate measures the real model, and torch.no_grad skips building the backward graph.

blocks.md: Now the loop that ties it all together. nanoGPT's `train.py` sets the learning rate from lesson 5's schedule, evaluates every `eval_interval` steps, saves a checkpoint when validation improves, and runs the micro-step loop. One detail: it fetches the next batch right after the forward pass, so on a GPU, where work runs asynchronously, loading the data overlaps the forward pass the GPU is still running.

blocks.title: train.py's main loop, simplified, with our run's real log values

scenes.caption: Step 0: warmup starts the learning rate at 1e-3 x 1/101 (lesson 5's formula with 100 warmup steps).
The first evaluation is the free sanity check from lesson 1: both splits at ln 65 = 4.17, as they should be with N(0, 0.02) weights.
One micro-step per iteration here (2,048 characters per step); GPT-2's config uses 40. Clip, step, then free the gradients.
Step 1,000: validation reaches its best value, 2.2482, so the checkpoint is written.
Step 2,000: train keeps falling, val climbs. No new best, no new checkpoint: ckpt.pt still holds step 1,000.
Step 3,000, the end: train 0.80, val 2.82. Without the best-val rule, this overfit model is what you would keep.

blocks.md: Why did it overfit? 100,000 characters is a small book, and 3,000 steps of 2,048 characters show the model each character about 61 times. The classic remedy is **dropout**, from the prerequisite course: during training each value is zeroed with probability $p$ (survivors are scaled by $1/(1-p)$), so the network cannot lean on any single activation. Lesson 3 listed where nanoGPT puts it; nanoGPT's Shakespeare config uses $p = 0.2$. We re-ran the identical setup with `--dropout=0.2`.

blocks.title: Same model and data, with and without dropout 0.2 (estimated loss)

scenes.caption: Step 0: identical starts at ln 65 = 4.17. (Train loss is measured in eval mode, so dropout never inflates it.)
Step 500: without dropout train is already lower (1.86 vs 2.04) and val too (2.32 vs 2.46). Dropout slows early learning.
Step 1,000: the no-dropout run hits its best val, 2.25. The gap between its train and val is now 0.73.
Step 2,000: no dropout has overfit (val 2.46 and rising); with dropout val is still falling, 2.29.
Step 3,000: val 2.82 against 2.27. Dropout's best val (2.267, at the last step) is still slightly worse than the no-dropout best (2.248) that the checkpoint saved.

blocks.md: Read the two runs together. Dropout did not buy a better best model here; it bought a run that does not degrade, which matters when you cannot evaluate often. The best-validation checkpoint did the rest, a form of **early stopping**. Check that it is on: nanoGPT's default `always_save_checkpoint = True` overwrites `ckpt.pt` after every evaluation, and only the Shakespeare config, which we used, sets it to False. Both are tools for small data. nanoGPT's GPT-2 config keeps the default `dropout = 0.0`; its comment says for pretraining 0 is good, for finetuning try 0.1+.

A **checkpoint** is everything needed to continue as if nothing happened. nanoGPT saves the model's state dict, the optimizer's state dict, the model arguments, `iter_num`, `best_val_loss` and the config. The optimizer part is not optional: AdamW keeps two running averages per parameter (its `exp_avg` and `exp_avg_sq`), so our 0.80M-parameter checkpoint is 9.7 MB, about 3.2 MB of weights plus 6.4 MB of Adam state. Starting with `init_from='resume'` restores all of it and continues at the saved `iter_num`, with the schedule picking up at the same learning rate.

Loss is not the only yardstick. build-nanogpt also tracks **HellaSwag**, a benchmark of sentence completions with four candidate endings each. The model scores each ending by its average per-token loss given the context and picks the lowest; random guessing gets 25%. Karpathy reports 29.5% for OpenAI's GPT-2 124M checkpoint and about 49% for GPT-2 XL, and 33.24% for build-nanogpt's own 124M model after about 40 billion training tokens.

A training loss far below validation loss is not progress. Watch the gap: once validation turns up while training keeps falling, more steps only memorize. Keep the best-validation checkpoint, add data, or add regularization such as dropout.

blocks.question: Your run logs train 0.95 and val 2.70 at step 4,000, after val bottomed at 2.31 at step 1,500. Which response fits?
options: Keep training: the train loss proves the model is still learning
Lower the learning rate, since rising val means the step size is too large
Use the step-1,500 checkpoint and, for the next run, add data or regularize (for example dropout)
Raise eval_iters, since the val number is just noise
blocks.explain: A val loss 0.39 above its own best, while train keeps falling, is overfitting, not noise: our estimates scatter by about 0.02 at most. The model has memorized its training text. Best-val checkpointing recovers the good model, and more data or dropout lets the next run go further before it turns.

blocks.question: Why does nanoGPT store OpenWebText as uint16 and not int64 like the tensors it trains on?
options: Every GPT-2 token id is at most 50,256, which fits in 16 bits, so the 9-billion-token file is 4 times smaller; get_batch converts each slice to int64
uint16 makes the tokenizer faster
PyTorch embeddings require 16-bit indices
Negative ids mark document boundaries
blocks.explain: Two bytes per token gives the 17 GB train.bin; int64 would be 72 GB. The conversion to int64 happens only for the few slices that get_batch reads. End-of-text is the ordinary id 50256, not a negative number.

lessons.title: Making it fast: TF32, bfloat16, torch.compile, fused attention and DDP

blocks.md: Here is the whole lesson in one measurement. In *Let's reproduce GPT-2*, Karpathy times one training step of the 124M model on 16 sequences of 1,024 tokens on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. In plain float32 it takes about 1,000 ms. After six changes, which leave the results the same up to floating-point rounding (one adds 47 never-used vocabulary rows), the same step takes about 90 ms, roughly 11 times faster. We walk through the changes in order. Our machine has no NVIDIA GPU, so every timing here is Karpathy's as reported in the video, not ours.

First, how to measure. The honest unit is **tokens per second**, $B \times T \times$ micro-steps $\times$ GPUs divided by the step time, because it stays comparable when the batch changes. One trap: PyTorch hands work to the GPU *asynchronously*, queueing kernels (single GPU programs) and returning at once, so a timer around Python code measures how fast you queued, not how fast the GPU ran. Call `torch.cuda.synchronize()` before reading the clock, and skip the first steps, which include one-time setup and compilation.

blocks.code:
import time
torch.set_float32_matmul_precision('high')          # TF32 matmuls
model = torch.compile(GPT(GPTConfig(vocab_size=50304)).to('cuda'))
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=6e-4, fused=True)
for step in range(50):
    t0 = time.time()
    x, y = train_loader.next_batch()                  # B=16, T=1024
    x, y = x.to('cuda'), y.to('cuda')
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    with torch.autocast(device_type='cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        logits, loss = model(x, y)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()                          # wait for the GPU to finish
    dt = time.time() - t0
    print(f"step {step} | {dt*1000:.0f} ms | {16*1024/dt:.0f} tok/s")
blocks.caption: A timing harness in the style of build-nanogpt's train_gpt2.py with all the speedups switched on; train_loader is its DataLoaderLite, which hands out consecutive B x T chunks of a token file. Not run here: it needs a CUDA GPU.

blocks.title: One A100, GPT-2 124M, 16 x 1,024 tokens: ms per step

scenes.caption: Baseline, everything in float32: about 1,000 ms per step, roughly 16,000 tokens per second.
TF32 matmuls: about 333 ms, 50,000 tokens per second. A 3x gain where the GPU's spec sheet promises 8x.
bfloat16 autocast: about 300 ms, 55,000 tokens per second. Small, because memory traffic, not arithmetic, is now the limit.
torch.compile: about 129 ms, 2.3x from one line, by fusing operations so fewer tensors make round trips to GPU memory.
scaled_dot_product_attention with is_causal=True (a Flash Attention kernel): about 96 ms, from about 130.
Vocabulary padded to 50,304, then the fused AdamW kernel: about 93 ms, then 90 ms. All values as reported in the video, eyeballed from its logs.

blocks.md: **TF32** (TensorFloat-32) is a format NVIDIA's tensor cores (the GPU's matrix-multiply units) use inside matrix multiplies: fp32's 8 exponent bits but only 10 stored mantissa bits. Inputs and outputs stay float32; only the internal products are rounded. One line turns it on, `torch.set_float32_matmul_precision('high')`, which PyTorch's docs say is equivalent to `allow_tf32 = True` on CUDA. The A100 figures Karpathy quotes are 19.5 TFLOP/s (trillion floating-point operations per second) for fp32, 156 for TF32 and 312 for bf16: the dense figures, not the doubled ones NVIDIA quotes for specially pruned sparse matrices.

blocks.prompt: TF32 matmuls are promised 8 times faster, yet the step only got 3 times faster. Why?
blocks.reveal: Most of a training step is not matrix multiplies. LayerNorms, GELU, softmax, residual additions and the optimizer each read whole tensors from GPU memory and write them back, and those tensors are still 4-byte floats. Those parts are **memory-bound**: they wait on bytes, not arithmetic, so faster multiplies cannot help them. That is why the next changes target memory traffic: 16-bit tensors (half the bytes) and fusion (fewer trips).

blocks.md: **bfloat16 autocast** is the prerequisite course's mixed precision: inside `torch.autocast(device_type='cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16)`, matrix multiplies run in bf16 while precision-sensitive ops such as softmax, LayerNorm and the loss stay in float32, and the parameters themselves stay float32. bf16 has fp32's exponent range, so unlike fp16 it needs no `GradScaler`; nanoGPT uses bfloat16 when the GPU supports it and falls back to float16 with a scaler otherwise.

**torch.compile** turns the model's Python code into optimized GPU kernels ahead of time. PyTorch's tutorial says the speedup mainly comes from reducing Python overhead and GPU read/writes. Take the tanh GELU from lesson 3: run op by op, each of its multiplies, adds and the tanh is a separate kernel that reads the whole (B, T, 3072) activation from GPU memory and writes a result back. Compiled, the chain becomes one kernel that reads the input once, does all the arithmetic in on-chip registers, and writes once.

blocks.title: Simplified: GELU op by op vs fused into one kernel

scenes.caption: Op by op, every elementwise step of 0.5 x (1 + tanh(c (x + 0.044715 x^3))) reads the full tensor and writes it back: memory passes pile up.

Compiled: one fused kernel, one read and one write. Same arithmetic, far fewer bytes moved. (Simplified: a real eager GELU is one built-in kernel; the point is the chain of small ops that compile fuses everywhere.)

blocks.md: **Fused attention.** Lesson 2's manual attention materializes a (12, 12, 1024, 1024) score tensor, about 302 MB per layer in 16-bit floats, and torch.compile does not rewrite it into a Flash Attention kernel by itself. Calling `F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)` lets PyTorch pick a fused kernel (its docs list FlashAttention-2 and a memory-efficient kernel on CUDA) that never stores that matrix. It even does more FLOPs, recomputing what it does not store, yet cut the step time by about 27%, from about 130 to 95 ms. On our CPU the fused call and the manual masked softmax agreed to within $7 \times 10^{-7}$.

**Nice numbers.** Padding the vocabulary from 50,257 to 50,304 ($786 \times 64$) adds 47 token rows that never occur in the data; the model quickly learns to push their logits toward minus infinity, and the GPU's kernels, which work in tiles sized by powers of two, no longer need a slow cleanup pass for the ragged remainder: 96.5 to 93 ms (Karpathy notes the gain was nearer 30% on PyTorch 2.3.1 and earlier). The **fused AdamW** (`fused=True`) updates all parameters in one kernel instead of a loop of small ones: 93 to 90 ms.

Then more GPUs. **DistributedDataParallel** (DDP) runs one process per GPU, launched by `torchrun`, which sets each process's `RANK`, `LOCAL_RANK` and `WORLD_SIZE`. Every process holds a full copy of the model and reads a different slice of the data. During `backward()`, DDP's reducer groups gradients into buckets and starts an **all-reduce** (a collective operation after which every process holds the same combined result, here the mean) on each bucket as soon as it is ready, overlapping communication with the rest of the backward pass. All replicas then take an identical optimizer step.

blocks.title: Two micro-steps on 3 GPUs with DDP (simplified)

scenes.caption: Micro-step 1: each rank runs forward and backward on its own micro-batch. Sync is off, so gradients just accumulate locally.
Micro-step 2, the last: sync is on. As each gradient bucket fills, DDP all-reduces it: every rank sends and receives pieces.
After the all-reduce every rank holds the same averaged gradient (shown as one more pass for simplicity).
Identical gradients and identical optimizer steps keep the replicas identical, with no weights ever sent.

blocks.code:
# launch: torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=8 train_gpt2.py
import os
from torch.distributed import init_process_group
from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP
init_process_group(backend='nccl')
rank, local_rank = int(os.environ['RANK']), int(os.environ['LOCAL_RANK'])
world_size = int(os.environ['WORLD_SIZE'])
torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank)
model = DDP(model.to(local_rank), device_ids=[local_rank])
grad_accum_steps = total_batch_size // (B * T * world_size)
for micro_step in range(grad_accum_steps):
    x, y = train_loader.next_batch()     # this rank's own slice of the data
    # all-reduce only on the last micro-step (what model.no_sync() toggles)
    model.require_backward_grad_sync = (micro_step == grad_accum_steps - 1)
    with torch.autocast(device_type='cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        logits, loss = model(x, y)
    (loss / grad_accum_steps).backward()
blocks.caption: The DDP lines from build-nanogpt's train_gpt2.py. Not run here (it needs several CUDA GPUs and NCCL, NVIDIA's communication library).

blocks.md: Gradient accumulation and DDP combine. Syncing on every micro-step would waste communication, so only the last micro-step all-reduces; build-nanogpt sets `require_backward_grad_sync`, the flag that DDP's `no_sync()` context manager toggles. The global batch is then micro-batch x $T$ x micro-steps x GPUs: $12 \times 1024 \times 5 \times 8 = 491{,}520$ tokens in nanoGPT's config, and $64 \times 1024 \times 1 \times 8 = 524{,}288 = 2^{19}$ in build-nanogpt's. On 8 A100s, Karpathy's run processed about 1.5 million tokens per second, 330 ms per step, so 19,073 steps (10 billion tokens) took about 1.7 hours.

blocks.caption: Lesson 5's FLOPs per token times measured throughput, over the GPU's peak. nanoGPT's estimate_mfu uses the A100's 312e12 bf16 peak.

blocks.md: Now lesson 5's formula pays off. With the padded vocabulary, nanoGPT's count (no position table) gives $N = 123{,}689{,}472$, so $6N + 12LHd_hT = 855{,}383{,}040$ FLOPs per token. At 1.5 million tokens per second over 8 GPUs that is $1.6 \times 10^{14}$ FLOP/s per GPU, an **MFU** of about 51% of 312 TFLOP/s. The float32 baseline, 16,384 tokens in about 1 s, works out to 4.5% of that bf16 peak; against the 19.5 TFLOP/s fp32 peak it would be 72%, so always say which peak an MFU uses. These are our calculations from Karpathy's reported throughput, not measurements.

Speedups are workload- and hardware-specific. The ladder above is one A100 at one batch shape; the same changes on another GPU, model size or PyTorch version give different factors. Measure your own tokens per second, after synchronizing, and change one thing at a time.

blocks.question: Which of these changes alters the numbers the model computes, not just how fast it computes them?
options: Switching from manual attention to scaled_dot_product_attention
Moving matmuls from float32 to TF32 or bfloat16
Wrapping the model in DDP with gradients averaged across 8 GPUs
Fusing AdamW into one kernel
blocks.explain: Lower-precision formats round the matmul inputs, so results differ slightly from float32; that is the accuracy traded for speed. Fused attention computes the same function (we saw agreement to 7e-7), DDP's averaged gradient equals one big batch's, and a fused optimizer does the same update.

blocks.question: You have 4 GPUs, micro-batch B = 16, T = 1024, and want build-nanogpt's 524,288 tokens per optimizer step. How many micro-steps must each GPU accumulate?
blocks.explain: 524,288 / (16 x 1024 x 4) = 8. Each GPU runs 8 micro-steps, all-reducing only on the last one, and the 4 GPUs together cover 524,288 tokens.

blocks.question: A run of GPT-2 124M processes 400,000 tokens per second on one GPU with a 989 TFLOP/s bf16 peak. Using 855 million FLOPs per token, what is its MFU?
options: About 86%
About 4%
About 35%
About 12%
blocks.explain: 400,000 x 855e6 = 3.42e14 FLOP/s, and 3.42e14 / 9.89e14 = 0.35. MFU compares useful model FLOPs to the hardware peak, the same calculation as for the A100 run.

lessons.title: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature, top-k and top-p

blocks.md: A trained GPT gives a distribution over the next token. **Generation** is a loop: run the model on the current context, take the logits at the **last** position only, turn them into probabilities, sample one token, append it, repeat. This is called *autoregressive* decoding, because each output becomes part of the next input.

blocks.title: nanoGPT's generate on the Shakespeare model (block_size 256)
blocks.code:
@torch.no_grad()
def generate(self, idx, max_new_tokens, temperature=1.0, top_k=None):
    for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
        bs = self.config.block_size
        idx_cond = idx if idx.size(1) <= bs else idx[:, -bs:]
        logits, _ = self(idx_cond)
        logits = logits[:, -1, :] / temperature
        if top_k is not None:
            v, _ = torch.topk(logits, min(top_k, logits.size(-1)))
            logits[logits < v[:, [-1]]] = -float('Inf')
        probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
        idx_next = torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=1)
        idx = torch.cat((idx, idx_next), dim=1)
    return idx

scenes.caption: Start from a 1 x 1 context holding token 0, the newline character, as the lecture does.
Context fits, so no crop. The forward pass (in inference mode) only computes lm_head for the final position.
Keep the last position's 65 logits and divide by the temperature.
Softmax, then draw one id at random in proportion to its probability (not the argmax).
Append and loop. After 256 new tokens idx has 257 columns.
Now the context is longer than block_size, so only the last 256 tokens are fed. wpe has just 256 rows, so the model cannot even represent position 256.

blocks.md: **Temperature** $\tau$ divides the logits before the softmax. $\tau<1$ sharpens the distribution toward the top choices; $\tau>1$ flattens it toward uniform. Why: softmax depends only on differences between logits, since $p_i/p_j = e^{(z_i-z_j)/\tau}$, and dividing by a temperature below 1 widens every gap. For logits 2 and 1 the ratio is $e^1 \approx 2.7$ at $\tau=1$, $e^2 \approx 7.4$ at $\tau=0.5$ and $e^{0.5} \approx 1.6$ at $\tau=2$. **Top-k** keeps only the $k$ largest logits, sets the rest to $-\infty$, and renormalizes, so very unlikely tokens can never be drawn. nanoGPT's `sample.py` exposes both (`--temperature`, `--top_k`).

blocks.caption: z are the logits of the final position; tau is the temperature.

blocks.title: Five candidate tokens with logits 2, 1, 0.5, 0, -1

scenes.caption: Temperature 1: the model's own distribution. A gets 56.3%, but 43.7% of the time something else is sampled.
Temperature 0.5: logits are doubled, so A rises to 82.9% and E drops to 0.2%. Text becomes safer and more repetitive.
Temperature 2: logits are halved, so A falls to 37.5% and E rises to 8.4%. Text becomes more varied and more error-prone.
Top-k = 2 at temperature 1: only A and B survive and are renormalized to 73.1% and 26.9%. The tail can never be drawn.
Top-k = 3 at temperature 0.8, both knobs together: 69.5%, 19.9%, 10.7%.

blocks.prompt: What does sampling become as the temperature goes toward 0, and as it grows very large?
blocks.reveal: As $\tau \to 0$ the largest logit dominates the softmax completely, so sampling becomes **greedy decoding**: always pick the argmax (nanoGPT would divide by zero at exactly 0, so you approximate with a tiny value). As $\tau \to \infty$ all logits divided by $\tau$ approach 0 and the distribution becomes uniform over the vocabulary, which produces noise.

blocks.md: Top-k uses the same $k$ whether the model is sure or unsure. **Nucleus sampling**, also called **top-p** (Holtzman et al., 2019), adapts to the distribution: sort the tokens by probability, keep the *smallest* set whose probabilities add up to at least $p$, renormalize, and sample. On our five logits the running sums are 56.3, 77.0, 89.6, 97.2 and 100%. With $p = 0.75$, A alone (56.3) is not enough and A plus B (77.0) is, so two tokens survive. With $p = 0.9$, A to C reach only 89.6, so D joins: four tokens, and only E is cut.

blocks.title: Top-p keeps fewer tokens when the model is sure

scenes.caption: Peaked logits (2, 1, 0.5, 0, -1) at temperature 1: the distribution from before.
Top-p 0.75: A and B together pass 75% (77.0), so only they survive, renormalized to 73.1 and 26.9.
Top-p 0.9: A to C sum to only 89.6, so D is needed: 57.9, 21.3, 12.9, 7.8. The tail token E is cut.
Now a flat step, logits (0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1, 0): the model is unsure. Probabilities 24.2, 21.9, 19.8, 17.9, 16.2.
Top-p 0.75 on the flat step keeps four tokens (83.8% cumulative), 28.9 to 21.4 after renormalizing. Top-k 2 would keep only A and B (52.5, 47.5) here as well as on the peaked step.

blocks.md: The motivation is the paper's title, *The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration*. Holtzman et al. found that decoding by maximizing probability (greedy or beam search) gives text that is bland and strangely repetitive, while pure sampling from the full distribution gives text that is incoherent and almost unrelated to the context, because the long tail of individually unlikely tokens adds up. On 5,000 continuations from GPT-2 Large, greedy decoding repeated itself in 73.66% of them against 0.28% for human text; nucleus sampling with $p = 0.95$ repeated in 0.36% and came closest to human perplexity (13.13 against 12.38).

Each new token reruns the model over the whole cropped context, even though the earlier positions' keys and values have not changed. nanoGPT accepts that cost for clarity. Production inference engines instead keep the **KV cache** from the attention course, the past keys and values of every layer, so each step only processes the new token, at the price of memory that grows with every generated token.

Generation also needs a way to stop. GPT-2 marks document boundaries with `<|endoftext|>`, id 50256, the token appended after every training document in lesson 6, so after a finished thought the model tends to predict it. Holtzman et al.'s continuations ended at an end-of-document token or after 200 tokens; Hugging Face's `generate` likewise stops at the model's end-of-sequence id, which is 50256 in GPT-2's configuration. nanoGPT's `generate` has no such check and always runs for exactly `max_new_tokens`.

The model never stores the text it generated anywhere except in `idx`. There is no hidden memory across calls: anything older than `block_size` tokens is simply cropped away and cannot influence the next prediction.

Training scores all positions in parallel with teacher forcing; generation is a sequential loop over the same network that samples from the last position's distribution, shaped by temperature, top-k or top-p.
Scaling this exact recipe up is how the GPT series grew: GPT-3 is an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters, still a stack of decoder blocks trained on next-token prediction.

blocks.question: Why does generate keep only `logits[:, -1, :]`?
options: Earlier positions' logits are always wrong
It saves memory and gives the same result as averaging all positions
Only the last position's logits predict the token that comes after the current context
The causal mask zeroes out the other positions' logits
blocks.explain: Position t's logits predict token t+1. Earlier positions predict tokens that already exist in the context, so they are useless here. The causal mask zeroes attention weights, not logits.

blocks.question: A sampling script uses `logits[logits <= v[:, [-1]]] = -inf` (note `<=`) with top_k = 5. What happens?
options: Nothing changes; < and <= behave the same
The 5th-largest logit (and any ties with it) is also removed, so only 4 tokens survive; with top_k = 1 every logit is masked and softmax returns NaN
Top-k now keeps 6 tokens
Temperature stops having an effect
blocks.explain: v[:, [-1]] is the k-th largest logit, the threshold that must survive. With <= it is thrown away too, leaving k - 1 choices, and for k = 1 nothing survives: all minus infinity gives NaN probabilities and multinomial fails.

blocks.question: At one step your model's distribution is very flat (hundreds of plausible tokens); at another it is very peaked (one token at 95%). Which setting adapts the candidate set to both?
options: Top-k with k = 40
Greedy decoding
Temperature 1.5
Top-p with p = 0.9
blocks.explain: Top-p keeps the smallest set reaching 90% of the mass: just one token when it alone holds 95%, hundreds when the distribution is flat. A fixed k = 40 is too many for the peaked case and may cut plausible options in the flat one; greedy ignores diversity; temperature reshapes but does not truncate.
